common_name: Nuccio's Jewel Camellia (White Formal Double Red-Streaked Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Jewel is a Nuccio's Nurseries formal double prized for its crisp white ground streaked and flecked with rose red.

directions: Site Nuccio's Jewel in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil where it is sheltered from midday sun, since strong glare fades the fine red streaking on its white petals. Flowers open in mid to late season as neatly imbricated formal doubles, with each bloom showing a slightly different pattern of red streaks against the white ground, making the plant a favorite for cut-flower displays. Keep a deep organic mulch over the root zone to buffer soil temperature and moisture swings, and water deeply during dry spells rather than allowing the shallow roots to dry out. Prune lightly right after bloom to shape the naturally upright, dense habit.

common_name: Nuccio's Bella Rossa Camellia (Bright Red Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Bella Rossa brings a heavy-flowering, glossy-leaved habit prized in nursery trade catalogs.

directions: Grow Nuccio's Bella Rossa in acidic, well-drained soil in bright, filtered shade, where its bright red semi-double to loose peony-form blooms show best against the dense, glossy dark green foliage. It is an unusually free-flowering selection, often producing so many buds that growers thin some in late winter to increase individual bloom size. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer just after flowering finishes and again in early summer, avoiding late-season fertilizing that can push tender growth into fall cold snaps. Mulch heavily to conserve moisture and moderate root temperatures through the Gulf Coast's hot summers.

common_name: Royal Velvet Camellia (Dark Red Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Royal Velvet is grown for its large, richly colored dark red blooms with a plush, velvety sheen.

directions: Plant Royal Velvet in acidic, well-drained soil under high, open shade so the deep red petals keep their velvety texture and rich color instead of bleaching in direct sun. Blooms are large semi-double to anemone-form flowers that open over a long midseason window on a compact, well-branched shrub. Keep the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged, and apply a thick pine straw or pine bark mulch to protect the shallow roots from summer heat. Watch for aphids on new growth flushes and treat promptly to keep foliage in show condition.

common_name: Nobilissima Camellia (Old-Fashioned White Formal Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nobilissima is a 19th-century European introduction still grown for its pristine white, early-season formal double flowers.

directions: Site Nobilissima in acidic, humus-rich soil in dappled or morning-only sun, since its snow-white petals bruise and brown quickly under harsh light or careless overhead irrigation. Flowers open very early in the camellia season as tightly imbricated formal doubles, a flower form this old European cultivar was originally bred to showcase on the exhibition table. Because early blooms are vulnerable to late cold snaps, plant in a site with some overhead canopy protection where flower buds are shielded from hard frost. Keep soil evenly moist with a generous mulch layer, and remove spent blooms promptly since browning white petals show more readily than on darker cultivars.

common_name: Prince Frederick William Camellia (Blush Pink Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this mid-1800s heirloom cultivar carries pale blush pink to white striped peony-form blooms.

directions: Grow Prince Frederick William in acidic, well-drained soil in filtered shade, where its blush pink petals, often streaked with deeper pink or white, are protected from harsh sun that can wash out the delicate coloring. The loose peony-form blooms open in midseason on a vigorous, upright plant that has remained in cultivation since the Victorian era for its dependable, generous flowering. Provide consistent moisture and a heavy organic mulch, and avoid planting in low spots where standing water can promote root rot in this older, less disease-tolerant heirloom line. Light structural pruning after bloom keeps the shrub full without sacrificing next season's buds.

common_name: Duchesse de Berry Camellia (French Heirloom Pale Pink Formal Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this 1830s French cultivar produces pale flesh-pink formal double flowers on a slow, dense-growing shrub.

directions: Plant Duchesse de Berry in rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving it room to develop its naturally dense, rounded form over many years. Blooms are pale pink formal doubles with fine imbricated petals, opening in midseason and holding their shape well, a legacy of its French formal-garden breeding origins. This older cultivar grows more slowly than modern hybrids, so be patient with young plants and avoid heavy pruning that removes future bud wood. Maintain even soil moisture and an acidic mulch layer, and protect from strong wind, which can bruise the closely packed petals.

common_name: Jupiter Camellia (Red Semi-Double Camellia japonica with Gold Stamens)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Jupiter bears bright red semi-double flowers with a prominent boss of golden stamens.

directions: Grow Jupiter in acidic, well-drained soil in dappled shade, where the bright red petals and conspicuous cluster of golden stamens stand out best against dark, glossy foliage. It flowers reliably in midseason on a vigorous, upright, free-branching plant that tolerates a bit more sun than many thinner-textured camellia cultivars. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist through the growing season, and fertilize with an acid-forming formula in spring and again after bloom. A sport of this cultivar with variegated petals is also grown, but the solid red form remains the more common garden selection.

common_name: Mars Camellia (Dark Red Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mars is a long-grown English cultivar valued for its large, dark red peony-form flowers.

directions: Place Mars in acidic, well-drained soil under high, filtered shade so its large, densely petaled dark red blooms open cleanly without sunscald on the outer petals. Flowering runs from early to midseason on a compact, well-shaped shrub that has remained a garden and show favorite for generations because of its reliable, heavy bud set. Water deeply and regularly during dry stretches, keep a thick mulch over the shallow root system, and thin crowded buds in winter if larger individual blooms are desired. Prune only lightly and only right after flowering to preserve next year's flower wood.

common_name: Commander Mulroy Camellia (Red and White Striped Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Commander Mulroy is an older cultivar prized for its bold red flowers boldly streaked with white.

directions: Grow Commander Mulroy in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the strong red-and-white streaking on its semi-double petals is easiest to appreciate against dark foliage. Bloom occurs in midseason and, like other genetically striped camellias, individual flowers can vary from mostly red to heavily white-streaked from year to year and even branch to branch. Keep soil moisture consistent and mulch heavily, since erratic watering tends to cause bud drop before these showy striped flowers can open fully. Prune to remove any all-white or all-red reverted shoots if you want to preserve the strongest striping in the planting.

common_name: Adelina Patti Camellia (Rose Pink and White Striped Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this 19th-century cultivar, named for the famed opera soprano, bears rose pink flowers streaked with white.

directions: Site Adelina Patti in acidic, well-drained soil in light shade, where the rose pink, white-streaked semi-double to loose peony-form flowers show their variable patterning to best effect. As an heirloom cultivar dating to the mid-1800s, it tends to grow more slowly and irregularly than modern hybrids, so allow extra years for the shrub to fill out. Keep the root zone evenly moist with a deep mulch, and feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring, since heavy feeding can push overly vigorous growth on this older, more measured-growing line. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the plant tidy and to reduce fungal issues in humid climates.

common_name: Alexander Hunter Camellia (Bright Red Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alexander Hunter is an Australian-raised cultivar known for its bright, clear red semi-double blooms.

directions: Grow Alexander Hunter in acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the vivid red semi-double flowers with their loosely arranged petals and visible golden stamens catch the eye without washing out. The plant is a vigorous, upright grower that flowers over a long midseason window and tends to set more buds than many exhibition-type cultivars, making it a dependable garden performer rather than strictly a show flower. Maintain consistent soil moisture and a thick organic mulch through summer heat, and prune lightly after bloom to keep the naturally open habit well filled. Watch for scale insects on older wood and treat promptly to protect vigor.

common_name: Gloire de Nantes Camellia (Rose Pink Semi-Double French Heirloom Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this French heirloom, distinct from the similarly named Ville de Nantes, bears large rose pink semi-double flowers.

directions: Plant Gloire de Nantes in rich, acidic, well-drained soil in filtered shade, where its large, clear rose pink semi-double flowers open reliably from early into midseason. Unlike the boldly variegated Ville de Nantes, this cultivar carries solid pink color, so gardeners should confirm labeling carefully when sourcing plants, since the two names are sometimes confused in the trade. It grows into a broad, well-branched shrub over time and tolerates a bit more cold than many later-flowering camellias, an asset for northern edges of camellia-growing country. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only right after bloom to preserve next season's buds.

common_name: Harriet Beecher Sheather Camellia (Rose Pink Formal Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Australian-raised cultivar produces rose pink formal double flowers with tightly arranged petals.

directions: Grow Harriet Beecher Sheather in acidic, well-drained soil under filtered shade, where its rose pink formal double blooms hold their neat, imbricated shape without sun-fading. Flowering occurs in midseason on a dense, compact shrub that is somewhat slower to establish than faster-growing hybrids but rewards patience with consistently well-formed flowers. Keep the root zone evenly moist with a heavy mulch layer, and feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and again after the bloom flush finishes. Light annual pruning right after flowering helps maintain a full, symmetrical shape suited to formal plantings.

common_name: Mercury Camellia (Carmine Rose Semi-Double Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mercury is a widely grown English cultivar noted for its large, carmine rose semi-double flowers.

directions: Site Mercury in acidic, well-drained soil in bright, dappled shade, where its large carmine rose flowers with a loose arrangement of broad petals and gold stamens show to full advantage. It blooms over a long midseason stretch on a vigorous, upright shrub that has been a garden mainstay for decades thanks to its combination of flower size and reliable bud set. Provide even moisture, a thick mulch layer, and an acid-forming fertilizer regimen in spring and after bloom to support its heavier-than-average flower production. Prune lightly right after flowering to control size, since the plant can become quite large if left unchecked for many years.

common_name: Bernhard Lauterbach Camellia (Red and White Striped German Heirloom Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this 1880s German-raised cultivar bears semi-double red flowers streaked and mottled with white.

directions: Grow Bernhard Lauterbach in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing the red-and-white streaked petals of its semi-double flowers to develop without stress that can cause reversion to solid color. As with other genetically striped camellias from this era of European breeding, the amount of white streaking can vary noticeably from bloom to bloom and season to season. Keep watering consistent and mulch deeply, since irregular moisture is a common cause of bud drop in older, less vigorous heirloom lines like this one. Prune out any branches that revert to solid red if you want to keep the planting's striped character prominent.

common_name: Annie Wylam Camellia (White Formal Double Camellia japonica with Pink Flecks)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Australian-raised, award-winning cultivar bears white formal double flowers lightly flecked with pink.

directions: Place Annie Wylam in acidic, well-drained soil in dappled or filtered shade, since its white formal double petals, occasionally flecked with soft pink, bruise easily in strong direct sun or careless overhead watering. Flowering occurs in midseason on a compact, densely branched plant that has earned recognition from horticultural societies for the precise, symmetrical arrangement of its petals. Keep the planting bed mulched and evenly moist, and remove faded blooms quickly since discoloration is more noticeable on pale flowers than on darker cultivars. Provide good air circulation to reduce petal blight risk in humid Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: Ann Blair Brown Variegated Camellia (Pink and White Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this variegated sport of the American-raised Ann Blair Brown carries rose pink petals splashed with white.

directions: Grow Ann Blair Brown Variegated in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the loose peony-form blooms display their characteristic rose pink and white marbling without excessive fading. As a color sport of the solid pink Ann Blair Brown, this selection can occasionally throw branches that revert to solid pink; prune these out if you want to preserve the variegated pattern throughout the shrub. It blooms in midseason on a vigorous, well-branched plant well suited to Southern gardens where the straight cultivar has long been a favorite. Maintain even soil moisture, a deep acidic mulch, and light post-bloom pruning to keep the plant shapely and floriferous.
